claim: Mosquitoes are major infectious disease-carrying vectors.
source: Mosquitoes are major infectious disease-carrying vectors.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about mosquitoes' role in disease transmission.

claim: Unbiased metatranscriptomic sequencing of individual mosquitoes offers a straightforward, rapid, and quantitative means to acquire information about pathogens and blood meal sources.
source: Unbiased metatranscriptomic sequencing of individual mosquitoes offers a straightforward, rapid, and quantitative means to acquire this information.
evidence: This claim is supported by the methodology and results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: 148 diverse wild-caught mosquitoes collected in California were profiled in this study.
source: Here, we profile 148 diverse wild-caught mosquitoes collected in California and detect sequences from eukaryotes, prokaryotes, 24 known and 46 novel viral species.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sequences from eukaryotes, prokaryotes, 24 known and 46 novel viral species were detected.
source: Here, we profile 148 diverse wild-caught mosquitoes collected in California and detect sequences from eukaryotes, prokaryotes, 24 known and 46 novel viral species.
evidence: This is supported by the taxonomic analysis and viral identification presented in the results.

claim: Sequencing individuals allowed speciation of host mosquito.
source: It allowed us to (a) speciate host mosquito
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparative whole transcriptome analysis described in the results.

claim: Sequencing individuals allowed computation of the prevalence of each microbe and recognition of a high frequency of viral co-infections.
source: (b) compute the prevalence of each microbe and recognize a high frequency of viral co-infections
evidence: This is supported by the prevalence data and co-infection analysis presented in the results.

claim: Sequencing individuals allowed association of animal pathogens with specific blood meal sources.
source: (c) associate animal pathogens with specific blood meal sources
evidence: This is demonstrated by the blood meal analysis and pathogen detection presented in the results.

claim: Simple co-occurrence methods were applied to recover previously undetected components of highly prevalent segmented viruses.
source: (d) apply simple co-occurrence methods to recover previously undetected components of highly prevalent segmented viruses.
evidence: This is supported by the co-occurrence analysis that identified novel viral genome segments.

claim: Mosquitoes are known to carry more than 20 different eukaryotic, prokaryotic, and viral agents that are pathogenic to humans.
source: Mosquitoes are known to carry more than 20 different eukaryotic, prokaryotic, and viral agents that are pathogenic to humans (WHO, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO 2017.

claim: Infections by mosquito-borne pathogens account for over half a million human deaths per year.
source: Infections by these mosquito-borne pathogens account for over half a million human deaths per year, millions of disability-adjusted life years (GBD 2017 Causes of Death Collaborators, 2018; GBD 2017 DALYs and HALE Collaborators, 2018; GBD 2017 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to GBD 2017 studies.

claim: Recent studies point to an increasing probability of a global expansion of mosquito habitat within the next two to three decades.
source: Moreover, recent studies of global patterns of urbanization and warming, as well as the possibility of mosquito transport via long-range atmospheric wind patterns point to an increasing probability of a global expansion of mosquito habitat and a potential concomitant rise in mosquito-borne diseases within the next two to three decades (Huestis et al., 2019; Kraemer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huestis et al., 2019 and Kraemer et al., 2019.

claim: Female mosquitoes take up blood meals from humans and diverse animals in their environment.
source: Female mosquitoes take up blood meals from humans and diverse animals in their environment and serve as a major source of trans-species introductions of infectious microbes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mosquito biology.

claim: Wolbachia has been shown to inhibit replication of various mosquito-borne, human-pathogenic viruses when introduced into susceptible mosquitoes.
source: For example, Wolbachia, a highly prevalent bacterial endosymbiont of insects (Werren et al., 2008) has been shown to inhibit replication of various mosquito-borne, human-pathogenic viruses when introduced into susceptible mosquitoes (Moreira et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Werren et al., 2008 and Moreira et al., 2009.

claim: Experimental releases of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes transinfected with Wolbachia have resulted in a significant reduction in the incidence of dengue virus infections in local human populations.
source: Experimental releases of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes transinfected with Wolbachia have resulted in a significant reduction in the incidence of dengue virus infections in local human populations.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding from previous research.

claim: Several recent, unbiased metagenomic analyses of batches of mosquito pools collected around the world have begun to address issues of mosquito microbiota composition.
source: Several recent, unbiased metagenomic analyses of batches of mosquito pools collected around the world have begun to address these issues (Atoni et al., 2018; Fauver et al., 2016; Frey et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Moreira et al., 2009; Pettersson et al., 2019; Sadeghi et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2016; Xia et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018a; Xiao et al., 2018b) (reviewed in Atoni et al., 2019; Xiao et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Key epidemiologic information needed to direct interventions is still lacking, including the measurement of viral prevalence within mosquito populations.
source: Despite these insights, key epidemiologic information needed to direct interventions is still lacking. This includes the measurement of viral prevalence within mosquito populations, their potential reservoir sources, or the impact that additional bacterial and eukaryotic microbes carried by mosquitoes might have on virus carriage, transmission, and pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of previous studies.

claim: Single mosquito analyses are required to link blood meal sources, endogenous microbes, and co-occurring pathogens.
source: Single mosquito analyses are required to link blood meal sources, endogenous microbes, and co-occurring pathogens.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the limitations of pooled analyses.

claim: Adult Aedes, Culex, and Culiseta mosquito species circulating in California in late fall of 2017 were collected.
source: Adult Aedes, Culex, and Culiseta mosquito species circulating in California in late fall of 2017 were collected to acquire a diverse and representative set of 148 mosquitoes for metatranscriptomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) analysis.
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology.

claim: Collections were targeted across a variety of habitats within five geographically distinct counties in Northern and Southern California.
source: We targeted collections across a variety of habitats within five geographically distinct counties in Northern and Southern California (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the text and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Primarily female mosquitoes were included to enrich for blood-feeding members of the population responsible for transmission of animal and human diseases.
source: Primarily female mosquitoes were included to enrich for blood-feeding members of the population responsible for transmission of animal and human diseases.
evidence: This describes the sampling strategy based on biological knowledge.

claim: A reference-free, kmer-based approach was applied to compute pairwise genetic distances between the complete metatranscriptomes acquired for each of the 148 mosquitoes.
source: Because complete genome sequences were not available for all mosquito species identified visually in this set, we applied a reference-free, kmer-based approach (Harris, 2018) to compute pairwise genetic distances between the complete metatranscriptomes acquired for each of the 148 mosquitoes.
evidence: This describes the computational methodology with a citation.

claim: Molecular groupings of mosquito genera and species agreed with visual calls for 95% of the specimens (n = 140/147).
source: These molecular groupings of mosquito genera and species agreed the visual calls for 95% of the specimens (n = 140/147, one sample had no visual identification).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparison of molecular and visual identification.

claim: Discordant calls occurred in contexts reported to present challenges to morphology-based speciation.
source: The discordant calls occurred in two contexts reported to present challenges to morphology-based speciation: (1) within the Culex genus in which genetic hybridization among species members has been documented and reported to confound accurate morphological speciation in California Cornel et al., 2003; Cornel et al., 2003; Kothera et al., 2012; McAbee et al., 2008; and (2) between samples belonging to the Culex and Culiseta genera that share some overlap in morphology, and require detection of features (perspiracular bristles and subcostal wing vein bristles) that can be lost or damaged during trapping and handling (Darsie and Ward, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies documenting these challenges.

claim: 77% of the 21.8 million non-host reads that assembled into contigs were classified to at least kingdom level.
source: In sum, we were able to classify, to at least kingdom level, 77% of the 21.8 million non-host reads that assembled into contigs with more than two reads.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the taxonomic classification analysis.

claim: The vast majority of the non-host reads that assembled into contigs corresponded to complete viral genomes (10.9 million reads of the 13 million total non-host reads assembled into contigs).
source: We found that the vast majority of the non-host reads that assembled into contigs corresponded to complete viral genomes (10.9 million reads of the 13 million total non-host reads assembled into contigs; Figure 2, all blocks in the treemap annotated with suffix '-viridae').
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by Figure 2.

claim: Positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses made up the most abundant class of detected viruses (7.4 million reads of the 10.9 million viral reads).
source: Positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses made up the most abundant class of detected viruses (7.4 million reads of the 10.9 million viral reads; Figure 2 blocks labeled Solemoviridae, Luteoviridae, Tombusviridae, Narnaviridae, Flaviviridae, Virgaviridae, and Iflaviridae)
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by Figure 2.

claim: A total of 70 distinct viral taxa were recovered, 46 of which correspond to distinctly divergent novel viruses.
source: In all, a total of 70 distinct viral taxa were recovered, 46 of which correspond to distinctly divergent novel viruses (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by Table 1.

claim: Only 10 of the 24 previously described viral taxa have been recovered from mosquitoes in California.
source: Intriguingly, only 10 of the 24 previously described viral taxa have been recovered from mosquitoes in California (Table 1, rows highlighted in gray; Chandler et al., 2015; Sadeghi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by Table 1 and citations to previous California studies.

claim: Members of Trypanosomatidae comprised more than 50% of eukaryotic reads (0.45M reads).
source: Members of Trypanosomatidae comprised more than 50% of these reads (0.45M reads), with a significant fraction assigned to the subfamily Leishmaniinae, that encompasses multiple Trypanosomatidae species known to infect insects and vertebrates.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the taxonomic analysis.

claim: Wolbachia comprised most of the prokaryotic reads (0.22 million reads).
source: Among the prokaryotic taxa detected, Wolbachia, a known endosymbiont of Culex quinquefasciatus (Werren et al., 2008), comprised most of the reads (0.22 million reads, Figure 2, bottom central row of brown-hued blocks).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by Figure 2 and a citation.

claim: Approximately 4.7 million reads corresponded to metagenomic 'dark matter', that is contigs without any recognizable sequence homology to previously published sequences.
source: A much larger fraction of non-host reads – approximately 4.7 million reads – corresponded to metagenomic 'dark matter', that is contigs without any recognizable sequence homology to previously published sequences.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sequence analysis.

claim: Twelve mosquitoes (8%) were found to harbor Trypanosomatidae taxa.
source: Twelve mosquitoes (8%) were found to harbor Trypanosomatidae taxa (Figure 3, bottom panel).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by Figure 3.

claim: Eight mosquitoes were identified with Apicomplexa contigs.
source: Within our single mosquito dataset, we identified eight mosquitoes with Apicomplexa contigs (Figure 3, bottom panel).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by Figure 3.

claim: Evidence of Nematoda carriage was seen in three Culex mosquitoes.
source: Finally, we examined taxa falling under Nematoda, a phylum that encompasses a diverse set of more than 50 filarial parasites of humans and animals. Here, we saw evidence of Nematoda carriage in three Culex mosquitoes: two Culex tarsalis and one Culex pipiens (Figure 3, bottom panel).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by Figure 3.

claim: 88% of mosquitoes harbored two or more (median 3) distinct viral taxa.
source: Importantly, among single mosquitoes, co-infections predominated, with 88% of mosquitoes harboring two or more (median 3) distinct viral taxa (Figure 4, panel A; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by Figure 4.

claim: Culex narnavirus one and Culex pipiens-associated Tunisia viruses were found at similar abundance in Culex erythrothorax mosquitoes, but the latter was three times more prevalent (30% vs 90%).
source: For example, Culex narnavirus one and Culex pipiens-associated Tunisia viruses were found at similar abundance in Culex erythrothorax mosquitoes obtained from the same collection site in West Valley; however, the latter was three times more prevalent (30% vs 90%, Figure 4, panel B; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by Figure 4.

claim: Wolbachia was detected in 32 mosquitoes belonging to Culex quinquefasciatus, Culex pipiens, and Aedes albopictus species.
source: Wolbachia was detected in 32 mosquitoes belonging to Culex quinquefasciatus, Culex pipiens, and Aedes albopictus species (Figure 3, middle panel, black bars and circle symbols).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by Figure 3.

claim: Blood meal calls fell into one of five broad categories: even-toed ungulates (Pecora), birds (Aves), carnivores (Carnivora), rodents (Rodentia), and rabbits (Leporidae).
source: For all samples, the blood meal call fell into one of five broad categories (Figure 5 and Figure 5—source data 1): even-toed ungulates (Pecora), birds (Aves), carnivores (Carnivora), rodents (Rodentia), and rabbits (Leporidae).
evidence: This is a result from the blood meal taxonomic classification supported by Figure 5.

claim: For 10 samples, blood meal genomic source was identified at the species level, including rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus), mallard duck (Anas platyrhynchos), and raccoon (Procyon lotor).
source: For 10 samples, we were able to identify the genomic source at the species level, including rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus), mallard duck (Anas platyrhynchos), and raccoon (Procyon lotor).
evidence: This is a result from the blood meal species identification.

claim: The only statistically significant association was between Pecora and Anaplasma (p=0.0005, Bonferroni corrected).
source: The only statistically significant association (p=0.0005, Bonferroni corrected) was between Pecora and Anaplasma, an intracellular erythroparasite transmitted by ticks.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the association analysis.

claim: Anaplasma was detected in 11 of the 20 samples with Pecora.
source: Anaplasma was detected in 11 of the 20 samples with Pecora.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the pathogen detection analysis.

claim: Co-occurrence analysis produced 27 candidate complete genomes for segmented viruses.
source: A cluster-by-sample heatmap for all segments co-occurring with RdRps resulted in 27 candidate complete genomes for segmented viruses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a result from the co-occurrence analysis supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Out of a total of 145 contig clusters, 75 were non-RdRp segments.
source: Out of a total of 145 contig clusters, 75 were non-RdRp segments.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the co-occurrence analysis.

claim: Of the 75 non-RdRp segments, 60 bore recognizable homology to their expected counterparts, and 15 were linked to recognizable partial genomes via co-occurrence.
source: Of these 75 non-RdRp segments 60 bore recognizable homology (colored in black) to their expected counterparts, based on associated RdRp segments and 15 were linked to recognizable partial genomes via co-occurrence.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the co-occurrence analysis.

claim: 15 putative segments lack homology to any known sequences at either nucleotide or amino acid level and may be part of viral genomes.
source: This supports the notion that the remaining 15 putative segments (colored in red), which lack homology to any known sequences at either nucleotide or amino acid level, may indeed be part of viral genomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-occurrence analysis.

claim: Four quaranjaviruses were identified in this study: Wuhan Mosquito Virus 6, Guadeloupe mosquito quaranja-like virus 1, Ūsinis virus, and Astopletus virus.
source: Quaranjaviruses are largely found in arthropods, and in this study, we identified four quaranjaviruses, two of which were previously observed in mosquitoes collected outside California (Wuhan Mosquito Virus 6 [WMV6; Li et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2017] and Guadeloupe mosquito quaranja-like virus 1 [GMQV1; Shi et al., 2019]) and two, which we have named Ūsinis virus and Astopletus virus, were previously unknown.
evidence: This is a result from the viral identification and classification, with citations for previously known viruses.

claim: Two additional segments (hypothetical 2 and hypothetical 3) were identified for WMV6.
source: Thus, for WMV6 and GMQV1 detected here, we observed all the previously identified segments (Li et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2017), as well as two additional segments (which we named hypothetical 2 and hypothetical 3) for WMV6
evidence: This is a result from the co-occurrence analysis with citations to previous studies.

claim: Five additional segments were identified for GMQV1 (PA, gp64, hypothetical, hypothetical 2, hypothetical 3).
source: and five for GMQV1 (PA, gp64, hypothetical, hypothetical 2, hypothetical 3) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, panels A - D).
evidence: This is a result from the co-occurrence analysis supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The existence of the two putative segments for WMV6 was confirmed by assembling homologous segments from reads in two previously published datasets.
source: We confirmed the existence of the two putative segments for WMV6 by assembling homologous segments from reads in two previously published datasets describing this virus.
evidence: This is a validation using external data.

claim: An 850 nucleotide contig cluster co-occurred with the Culex narnavirus 1 RdRp segment in more than 40 mosquitoes collected from diverse locations across California.
source: A striking example is an 850 nucleotide contig cluster that co-occurred with the Culex narnavirus 1 RdRp segment in more than 40 mosquitoes collected from diverse locations across California (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a result from the co-occurrence analysis supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The putative new second segment of Culex narnavirus 1 shares the exceptional feature of ambigrammatic open reading frames.
source: Like the RdRp segment, the putative new second segment shares the exceptional feature of ambigrammatic open reading frames (ORFs), that is a distinct ORF encoded by the reverse complementary RNA strand (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, panel E).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nearly identical contigs to the Culex narnavirus 1 Robin segment were recovered from previously published mosquito datasets, all of which also contained the Culex narnavirus 1 RdRp segment.
source: Moreover, we were able to recover nearly identical contigs from previously published mosquito datasets, all of which also contained the Culex narnavirus 1 RdRp segment.
evidence: This is a validation using external data.

claim: There was no significant co-occurrence between Culex narnavirus one and a non-mosquito eukaryotic taxon.
source: However, there was no significant co-occurrence with a non-mosquito eukaryotic taxon, or between the abundance of Culex narnavirus one and abundance of fungi (Figure 6—figure supplement 5 and Figure 6—figure supplement 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from the co-occurrence analysis supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: It is likely that mosquitoes serve as direct hosts of the Culex narnavirus 1.
source: Thus, it is likely that mosquitoes serve as direct hosts of the Culex narnavirus 1, whose genomes we show here consist of two, still enigmatic, ambigrammatic RNA segments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of co-occurrence with other eukaryotes.

claim: The genome of a large clade of quaranjaviruses consists of 8 segments.
source: Using this approach, we identified previously unknown genome segments establishing that the genome of a large clade of quaranjaviruses (those descended from the common ancestor of WMV6 and GMQV1), like distantly related influenza A and B viruses, consists of 8 segments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-occurrence analysis and phylogenetic inference.

claim: 7% of the reads in the metagenomic 'dark matter' fraction were pulled into the light through co-occurrence analysis.
source: In sum, we pulled 7% of the reads in the metagenomic 'dark matter' fraction of our dataset into the light.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the co-occurrence analysis.

claim: The clusters from molecular identification were 95% concordant with the visual mosquito species calls.
source: Field validation of which mosquito species carry which pathogens in a specific geographic area informs targeted analysis and control of that species (Petersen et al., 2013). Here, though only 3 of the 10 collected mosquito species had complete genome references, it was possible to estimate pairwise SNP distances between samples in a reference-free way and perform an unsupervised clustering. The clusters were 95% concordant with the visual mosquito species calls, and discordant outliers were easy to detect and correct.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the molecular species identification with a citation.

claim: The prevalence of viruses ranged from detection in one mosquito to detection in all 36 Culex tarsalis samples in the study.
source: We found the prevalence of viruses ranged from detection in one mosquito (peribunya-like Udune virus) to detection in all 36 Culex tarsalis samples in the study (Marma virus).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the prevalence analysis.

claim: A significant fraction (n = 46) of the 70 viral genomes identified correspond to novel divergent viruses.
source: A significant fraction (n = 46) of the 70 viral genomes we identified in this study correspond to novel divergent viruses.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the viral identification.

claim: Known mosquito-borne human pathogens known to circulate in California (West Nile Virus, St. Louis Encephalitis Virus, Western Equine Encephalitis Virus) were not detected.
source: Among the 24 previously described viral genomes we recovered, we did not detect any of the known mosquito-borne human pathogens known to circulate in California (West Nile Virus, St. Louis Encephalitis Virus, Western Equine Encephalitis Virus).
evidence: This is a result from the viral detection analysis.

claim: 10 of the 24 previously described viruses recovered correspond to viral agents described in a recent bulk mNGS of approximately 12,000 mosquitoes collected in California in 2016 or an mNGS study of seven single mosquitoes collected in 2013.
source: In contrast, 10 of the 24 previously described viruses we recovered in this study correspond to viral agents described in a recent bulk mNGS of approximately 12,000 mosquitoes collected in California in 2016 (Table 1, Sadeghi et al., 2018) or an mNGS study of seven single mosquitoes collected in 2013 (Chandler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies supported by Table 1 and citations.

claim: Detection of a potential blood meal host in 45/60 of the blood engorged mosquitoes via RNA-based mNGS analysis is encouraging.
source: Detection of a potential blood meal host in 45/60 of the blood engorged mosquitoes via RNA-based mNGS analysis is encouraging, especially in light of additional evidence of accompanying microbial cargo.
evidence: This is an evaluation of the blood meal detection results.

claim: Complementing conventional analyses with single mosquito mNGS can provide valuable complementary information to enhance the evidence base for interventions to control mosquito-borne infectious diseases.
source: In sum, complementing conventional analyses of mosquito pools and field observations of mosquitoes and the animals they bite with single mosquito mNGS can provide valuable complementary information to enhance the evidence base for distinct interventions to control mosquito-borne infectious diseases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.
